summary: Steel light at the end of Manitowoc's north breakwater: a frame fog-signal station from 1895, a steel tower from 1918, and a private owner since 2010.

structures.type: steel light tower on a concrete basement
structures.note: Fourth-order lens when new (LighthouseFriends); fog-signal diaphone added 1919.

structures.type: frame building with corrugated iron covering
wooden pierhead tower on the stub of the old north pier
structures.note: Pierhead light moved to the stub in 1907; electrified 1921; destroyed by a storm in 1938.

access.note: Privately owned. Grounds open, tower closed (LighthouseFriends).

visit.note: Tours arranged with the owner by the Manitowoc Sunrise Rotary Club since 2019; lens on display at the Wisconsin Maritime Museum.

events.note: Breakwater light and frame fog-signal station. Sources differ on the day in November (11, 28 or 30).
10-inch steam whistle; the Board's text gives 28 November 1895 and its list gives 30 November.
Light and fog signal moved 400 ft southeast on the breakwater.
Breakwater light moved 500 ft shoreward after the outer breakwater was removed.
January 1908 wind storm; the assistant on duty was stranded at the station and reached shore by tug.
Ross F. Wright commended for helping a party in a disabled motor boat. LighthouseFriends dates the rescue 1913.
Steel tower on a concrete basement; the 1917 appropriation was for a new steel station.
Old frame fog-signal structure removed from the breakwater.
Fourth-order Fresnel per LighthouseFriends; the USLHS record gives 1918.
Permanent light, 13 December 1919, after a temporary oil light on 15 November 1918.
Type F diaphone fog signal, same date as the permanent light.
Keepers rescued two airmen after an exhibition seaplane fell into the harbor on Navy Day (LighthouseFriends only).
Wooden pierhead tower on the north pier stub electrified.
Wooden pierhead tower destroyed by a storm.
Skeletal tower replaced the destroyed wooden tower.
Fifth-order lens removed and placed on display at the Wisconsin Maritime Museum.
Put up for federal auction on 18 October 2010; the minimum bid was $25,000 and the sale closed in December 2010.
Renovated and painted before the 2018 centenary, at a reported cost of about $325,000.

corrections.why: The tower built in 1918 is steel: the 1917 appropriation was for a 'New steel fog-signal and light station' (Commissioner's report) and LighthouseFriends describes a steel-plate tower on a concrete basement. The wooden tower was the 1873 pierhead light on the north pier, electrified in 1921 and destroyed in 1938.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: USLHS gives 1918 as the year the station was established. The Board's report of 1896 shows a breakwater light and frame fog signal already in service in November 1895. The 1918 date is the steel station that replaced the frame building.

The Manitowoc Pilot of January 1908 names the assistant in the storm 'Edward Warren'. The USLHS roster and LighthouseFriends name Joseph E. Warren, first assistant 1906 to 1911. The story uses the roster name and reports the paper's variant.

The Lighthouse Service Bulletin of 1912 reports Ross F. Wright's commendation for helping a party in a disabled motor boat. LighthouseFriends describes a 1913 rescue by Wright of a party of boys and girls adrift on Lake Michigan. Its account does not say whether it is the same event, so the story does not assume so.

notes_for_editor: Dates for the 1895 breakwater light and fog signal differ: the Board's list gives 11 November 1895 for the light, its text gives 28 November for the whistle and its list gives 30 November; LighthouseFriends gives 28 November for both. The steel tower is USLHS 1918 and LighthouseFriends' temporary light 1918, permanent light 13 December 1919. Wikipedia's infobox gives 1918 first lit; not cited. LighthouseFriends is a community site and is cited for facts only; the 1919 seaplane rescue, the 1921-1938 wooden tower history, the 1935 dwelling, the 1964 diaphone, the 2002 lens removal, the 2010 auction and the 2018 restoration rest on it alone, and the seaplane rescue was not found in Chronicling America for August 1919 (searched Walker/seaplane/Manitowoc, Wisconsin, 1919). The lens order is inconsistent within LighthouseFriends (fourth order in 1919, fifth order in 2002); the story says so. Keeper names matched by the roster (USLHS) are as printed, including 'Napiezinski'/'Napeizinski' and 'Jen J. Rollefson'. Coast Guard keepers after 1960 are in the roster but not named in the story. The Manitowoc Pilot OCR reads the 1908 assistant as 'Edward Warren'; the image was not checked. Shape: six chapters at about 940 words, which is moderate length (the guide's moderate shape is 2-4 chapters); the editor may collapse the shape. Fact-check 2026-10-27: the 1915 Napeizinski line is in the Commissioner's 'Saving of Life and Property' table (scan p. 69), not a keeper list; the story now says so and cites that page. That table is OCR'd in columns: the name was matched by column position and the vessel column was not matched, and the page image was not read. The Pilot's 'Edward Warren' is read from running text (checked against the OCR, image not viewed). LighthouseFriends' 'remained at the station all day' is a newspaper passage that LF prints, not LF's own words, and the story now says so. The 1912 commendation and LighthouseFriends' 1913 rescue may or may not be the same event. The 1908 OCR matches the story.
